newsitem.title: FINLAND: U.S. says nuclear arms control progress at summit.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says nuclear arms control progress at summit.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin made significant progress on nuclear arms control on Friday, holding out the prospect of deeper cuts in their arsenals, a senior U.S. official said.
"On arms control we were able to move the ball forward in a significant way," the official told Reuters.

The official said the two presidents had agreed negotiations on a further cut in strategic nuclear weapons should go ahead and that Yeltsin had given a commitment to get a long-delayed nuclear arms treaty ratified by the Russian parliament.

It was unclear if this implied the United States meant talks on a new round of nuclear cuts should go ahead regardless. Until now, Washington has said the delayed 1993 START-2 treaty must be ratified first by the parliament (Duma) in Moscow.

It is also not clear whether Yeltsin will be able to get the treaty past his communist and nationalist opponents in parliament, who have held up giving their approval to the agreement because they say it harms Russia's security.

START-2 aims to cut U.S. and Russian warheads for long-range missiles to no more than 3,500 on each side, about a third of their Cold War level. Washington has said a new round of talks would aim to make even deeper cuts, to between 2,000 and 2,500 on each side.
